source.title: Don't Cut Corners: Exact Conditions for Modularity in Biologically Inspired Representations
source.authors: Will Dorrell; Kyle Hsu; Luke Hollingsworth; Jin Hwa Lee; Jia-Jun Wu; Chelsea Finn; Peter E. Latham; T. Behrens; James C. R. Whittington

page_placements.theme: Units mix features without capacity pressure

record.tranche_reason: The study refines accounts of mixed selectivity: its results show that some apparent mixing can arise when an encoded source is omitted from analysis, while other mixing arises in models when source ranges are dependent.
record.gate_note: The study measures modularity and mixed selectivity in its own trained networks, including the effect of conditioning on known versus omitted sources. It does not examine InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, transformer MLP neurons, or neuron feature visualizations. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study offers its own results and theory on when neurons in trained networks mix variables rather than encode one each. In its biologically constrained toy networks, mixing arises from range-dependent source support even with more neurons than sources. Regularization and nonnegativity change the amount of mixing. An analysis that omits an encoded variable makes modular neurons look mixed. The construct is mixed selectivity over task source variables in small networks, not polysemanticity in image classifiers or language models. Links are therefore limited to V4, V5 and V7, the versions whose wording is not tied to model type.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for when optimal nonnegative, energy-efficient linear autoencoders modularise: the source support must be 'sufficiently spread', roughly rectangular. Range independence, not statistical independence, drives modularity, and this extends empirically to nonlinear feedforward and recurrent networks and to entorhinal data. They suggest two alternative origins of mixed selectivity: energy-efficient encoding of range-dependent variables, and spurious mixing when analyses omit encoded correlated variables.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theory about source support and conditional-information measurements in biologically constrained feedforward and recurrent networks, rather than neuron activation visualizations or feature-level inspection of image classifiers.
record.method_sensitivity: Modularity changes with source support and reward-position range dependence. Apparent selectivity also changes according to whether the analysis conditions on all encoded sources or omits one.

fits_no_version.finding: In biologically constrained networks with more neurons than sources, mixing is governed by source range/support (missing joint extremes), not by statistical dependence or capacity. Multiinformation does not predict mixing (Fig 1c).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixed or polysemantic units can be energy-optimal when encoded variables are range-dependent, independent of capacity pressure.

record.problems: The paper does not report a prevalence estimate for polysemantic neurons or inspect canonical AI polysemantic units. Several relevant empirical outcomes are described qualitatively in text or figures rather than with numerical values in the text; the What-Where experiments report five random seeds, but the specific outcomes cataloged here have no stated uncertainty.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or InceptionV1 units examined.
No transformer language models or MLP neurons; no prevalence or layer profile.
Superposition and features-outnumbering-neurons are not tested. The study's settings all have more neurons than sources.
No SoLU, convnet or activation-function comparison. No share of polysemantic neurons reported; the tested network is a 25-unit toy.
No canonical polysemantic neurons revisited. No estimate of how often apparent mixtures are misreadings.
Activation-range slices and explanation-scoring methods are not varied. Only the choice of conditioning variables is tested.

missing.what: Linear autoencoder test: the degree to which the inequalities are broken predicts the most-mixed neuron's angle; source multiinformation does not. Removing a single datapoint flips the network from modular to mixed.
Linear and nonlinear RNNs: harmonic frequency pairs mix, while irrational or non-harmonic rational pairs modularise (hidden size 16).
Teacher-student RNNs: removing corners breaks modularity, sparsifying corners breaks it more slowly, and statistical dependence alone preserves it.
Lowering the reconstruction penalty makes a range-independent four-point dataset mix, so the result depends on the loss tradeoff.

record.verdict_notes: A neuroscience-oriented paper on modularity versus mixed selectivity. Sources are task variables in small toy networks, so the bearing on polysemantic-neuron claims about large AI models is indirect; researchers should weigh the construct gap. The reader's V6 links were moved to V4 (R3–R7) and to V7 only (R8–R9). All key results are qualitative or figure-based, with no numerical mixing shares in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or InceptionV1 units are examined.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, or language contexts are examined.
The study does not test superposition or whether feature count exceeds neuron count.
The study does not test polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise under sufficient capacity.

The study tests biological constraints in a feedforward task, but does not compare SoLU, modern convnet architectures, or a broad range of activation functions. It does not report a general share of polysemantic neurons.

The study demonstrates an omitted-source analysis artifact and also models genuine mixing under range dependence. It does not revisit canonical polysemantic units such as InceptionV1 4e:55 or establish how often mixtures in trained AI models are artifacts.
The study tests the effect of conditioning on known versus omitted sources; it does not vary activation-range slices or compare explanation-scoring methods.

conditions.value: corner cutting versus changes that preserve rectangular support, including diagonal dropout or added correlations

rows.baseline: Distributions preserving rectangular support; the independent-source case is reported as modular.
rows.value: Corner cutting severely degrades modularity; changing source dependence while preserving the rectangular support affects modularity less.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the mean shown as shaded regions in Figure 2; numerical values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors interpret the result as mixing associated with source-range dependence, not as evidence that mixed units are mostly artifacts.
rows.check: Relinked from V6 to V4. Corner cutting produces mixing in a 25-unit net with 2 sources (surplus capacity) under activity/weight regularization, which is what V4 names. It does not bear on V6, which concerns canonical units being misread. State for V4 is observed, not partial.

rows.subject: Linear RNN for position and reward displacement
rows.operation_detail: Measured whether the learned representation separates spatial and reward-vector information across room reward arrangements.

conditions.value: some rooms have randomly scattered rewards and others have fixed reward locations

rows.measure: Qualitative modularity of spatial and reward-vector representations
rows.value: The representation stays modular when random-reward rooms are present.
rows.note: The study describes the random and fixed reward arrangements as range-independent when both occur across rooms.
rows.check: Relinked from V6 to V4. With range-independent but correlated reward and position, regularized surplus-capacity RNNs stay modular, so no mixing arises.

rows.subject: Linear RNN for position and reward displacement
rows.operation_detail: Measured whether the learned representation separates spatial and reward-vector information when all rooms have fixed reward locations.

conditions.value: all sampled rooms have fixed reward positions

rows.baseline: Modular representation when some rooms have randomly scattered rewards.
rows.value: Neurons become mixed selective to reward and self-position.
rows.note: The authors attribute this mixing to range dependence between reward and position.
rows.check: Relinked from V6 to V4. Mixing appears only once every room has fixed rewards (range dependence).

rows.subject: Linear RNN for displacement to three objects
rows.operation_detail: Measured linear conditional information between neuron activity and object outputs, conditioning on all three objects.

conditions.value: all three encoded objects are known and included in the conditioning

rows.measure: Linear NCMI between neural activity and object output codes
rows.value: Each neuron is reported as informative about a single source.
rows.note: The three object positions are range-independent but correlated.
rows.check: This is the baseline analysis condition for V7. Removed from V6. Under full conditioning the neurons are modular.

rows.subject: Linear RNN for displacement to three objects
rows.operation_detail: Recomputed linear conditional information while treating only two of the three encoded objects as known.

conditions.value: third encoded object omitted from the variables used for conditioning

rows.measure: Linear NCMI between neural activity and the two included object outputs
rows.baseline: With all three objects included, neurons are reported as informative about a single source.

rows.note: The authors present this as an analysis artifact caused by omitted, correlated sources.
rows.check: Removed from V6: no canonical polysemantic unit is revisited, and the setup is planted (synthetic correlations by design). For V7 it shows that the classification flips with the choice of conditioning variables.

source_check.notes: The text is arXiv v4, retitled 'Range, not Independence, Drives Modularity in Biologically Inspired Representations'; the catalog uses the older 'Don't Cut Corners' title. It studies mixed selectivity over 2-6 sources in biologically constrained toys, not AI polysemantic neurons. Capacity is never varied, though the theory's conditions hold for any dz > ds. In the feedforward nets, range-preserving correlations still add some mixing.

statements.problem: Minor: the conditions line puts QLAE among 'nonnegative' networks. QLAE uses weight decay and quantised latents, not nonnegativity. The Section 5 RNN's hidden size is not stated, so surplus capacity there is inferred.

statements.correction: arXiv:2410.06232#R6: linear RNN, non-negative activities, L2 penalty on activity and all weight matrices (Appendix H.3); lambda and hidden size not stated. Elsewhere in the study: What-Where uses ReLU plus L2 on weights and activity (lambda_R 0.01); QLAE uses weight decay 0.1 plus quantised latents.
statements.problem: differences_stated calls this study's regularization 'unspecified'. The text specifies it. The cited row R6 is a linear RNN trained with an L2 penalty on activity and on all weight matrices, plus non-negative activities.
Right for R6 (RNN). Note that in the nonlinear feedforward nets, correlations that keep rectangular support still add some mixing, less than corner cutting (Section 3, Fig 2a).

statements.correction: arXiv:2410.06232: supervised What-Where regression net (81 inputs, 25 hidden units, 2 outputs). Measure: qualitative hidden-unit weights and tuning (Appendix F.2.1, Figs 10-11), with no count of mixed units. Negligible loss is stated across all settings (F.1.3).
statements.problem: The 'what' part about this study is right. But the conditions line gives the proxy as superposition geometry or MCC in autoencoders/encoders. This study's evidence is qualitative hidden-unit tuning in a supervised What-Where regression net.
